evidence.excerpt: The Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa
Having bowed down to Narayana and Nara, the most exalted male being, and also to the goddess Saraswati
Ugrasrava, the son of Lomaharshana, surnamed Sauti, well-versed in the Puranas
the great sages of rigid vows, sitting at their ease, who had attended the twelve years' sacrifice of Saunaka, surnamed Kulapati, in the forest of Naimisha.
one of the Rishis beginning the conversation, asked him, 'Whence comest thou, O lotus-eyed Sauti, and where hast thou spent the time?
Accomplished in speech, Sauti, thus questioned, gave in the midst of that big assemblage of contemplative Munis a full and proper answer
the diverse sacred and wonderful stories which were composed in his Mahabharata by Krishna- Dwaipayana
which were recited in full by Vaisampayana at the Snake-sacrifice of the high-souled royal sage Janamejaya and in the presence also of that chief of Princes, the son of Parikshit
where formerly was fought the battle between the children of Kuru and Pandu, and all the chiefs of the land ranged on either side.
The Rishi replied, 'The Purana, first promulgated by the great Rishi Dwaipayana
just as it was cheerfully recited by the Rishi Vaisampayana, under the direction of Dwaipayana himself, at the snake-sacrifice of Raja Janamejaya?
Having bowed down to the primordial being Isana, to whom multitudes make offerings, and who is adored by the multitude; who is the true incorruptible one, Brahma
who is the creator of high and low; the ancient, exalted, inexhaustible one; who is Vishnu, beneficent and the beneficence itself
who is Hari, the ruler of the faculties, the guide of all things moveable and immoveable

in which we are told, was the true light Brahma, the eternal one, the wonderful and inconceivable being present alike in all places; the invisible and subtile cause, whose nature partaketh of entity and non-entity.
From this egg came out the lord Pitamaha Brahma, the one only Prajapati; with Suraguru and Sthanu.
Then appeared the twenty-one Prajapatis, viz., Manu, Vasishtha and Parameshthi; ten Prachetas, Daksha, and the seven sons of Daksha.
Then appeared the man of inconceivable nature whom all the Rishis know
The sons of Div were Brihadbhanu, Chakshus, Atma Vibhavasu, Savita, Richika, Arka, Bhanu, Asavaha, and Ravi.
Of these Vivaswans of old, Mahya was the youngest whose son was Deva-vrata. The latter had for his son, Su-vrata
Su-vrata who, we learn, had three sons,--Dasa- jyoti, Sata-jyoti, and Sahasra-jyoti, each of them producing numerous offspring.
The illustrious Dasa-jyoti had ten thousand, Sata-jyoti ten times that number, and Sahasra-jyoti ten times the number of Sata-jyoti's offspring.
From these are descended the family of the Kurus, of the Yadus, and of Bharata; the family of Yayati and of Ikshwaku; also of all the Rajarshis.
Some read the Bharata beginning with the initial mantra (invocation), others with the story of Astika, others with Uparichara

The son of Satyavati having, by penance and meditation, analysed the eternal Veda, afterwards composed this holy history, when that learned Brahmarshi of strict vows, the noble Dwaipayana Vyasa, offspring of Parasara, had finished this greatest of narrations
Brahma, the world's preceptor, knowing of the anxiety of the Rishi Dwaipayana, came in person to the place where the latter was
And Vyasa having gone round him who is called Hiranyagarbha seated on that distinguished seat stood near it; and being commanded by Brahma Parameshthi
Then the greatly glorious Vyasa, addressing Brahma Parameshthi, said, "O divine Brahma, by me a poem hath been composed which is greatly respected.
and the all-pervading spirit;--all these have been represented.
Let Ganesa be thought of, O Muni, for the purpose of writing the poem.
Brahma having thus spoken to Vyasa, retired to his own abode.
And Ganesa, obviator of obstacles, ready to fulfil the desires of his votaries, was no sooner thought of, than he repaired to the place where Vyasa was seated.
Ganesa, upon hearing this address, thus answered, 'I will become the writer of thy work, provided my pen do not for a moment cease writing." And Vyasa said unto that divinity
I am (continued Sauti) acquainted with eight thousand and eight hundred verses, and so is Suka, and perhaps Sanjaya.

unresolved: The invocation explicitly identifies Isana with Brahma, Vishnu and Hari. It does not explicitly link that referent to the true-light Brahma, Pitamaha Brahma emerging from the egg, or Brahma visiting Vyasa. Those references are retained separately pending evidence establishing identity; this does not assert that they are different beings.

The candidate's combined creation-and-visit Brahma entry has been separated because the batch does not explicitly establish that Pitamaha Brahma and the visiting Brahma are identical. Hiranyagarbha and Brahma Parameshthi are explicitly connected within the visit scene.
Parameshthi is explicitly named in the Prajapati list, so that mention is supported. Its identity with the visiting Brahma Parameshthi remains unresolved.

The supplied list prints Atma Vibhavasu without a separating comma. Whether this denotes one individual or separate individuals named Atma and Vibhavasu cannot be settled from this batch. The combined source label and its parent relationship are therefore provisional.

Mahya is called the youngest of these Vivaswans but is absent from the preceding enumeration of Div's sons. Div's parentage of Mahya and Mahya's sibling relationships to the enumerated sons depend on resolving that reference and remain provisional.
Sibling relationships are deductions from the listed common parentage, not explicit statements using a sibling term. Each symmetric pair is recorded once and marked provisional.

The all-pervading spirit is a singular reference in Vyasa's catalogue, but the passage does not establish whether it denotes an individual being or a philosophical principle. Its entity entry is provisional, with no identification to another entry.

The seven sons of Daksha, ten Prachetas, twin Aswins, children of Kuru and Pandu, other collective classes, and counted offspring of the three Jyotis are not individually distinguished in this batch. Counts and collective labels have not been converted into individual entities.

The descent claim concerns families and unspecified generations. It does not establish direct parent_of relationships to Bharata, Yayati or Ikshwaku. The plural Yadus does not establish an individually named Yadu.
Parentage does not establish the genders of Satyavati, Parasara, Lomaharshana or Parikshit in this batch, or a spouse relationship between Satyavati and Parasara.

People mentioned only as translators, editors, commentators, literary authors, patrons or other participants in the translator's preface are outside the epic narrative inventory. Book and poem titles alone have not been converted into character mentions.

matches.reason: Both passages explicitly identify Dwaipayana Vyasa as a Brahmarshi and offspring of Parasara.
Both identify Ugrasrava as the narrator surnamed Sauti and the son of Lomaharshana.
Both identify Lomaharshana through parentage of the same Ugrasrava, surnamed Sauti.
Both passages name Saunaka, surnamed Kulapati, in connection with the twelve-year sacrifice.
Both identify the snake-sacrifice Janamejaya as the son of Parikshit. This distinguishes him from the existing Janamejaya whose parents are Puru and Kausalya.

CURRENT identifies Parikshit through his son, the snake-sacrifice Janamejaya. The existing genealogical excerpts continue directly from naming Abhimanyu and Uttara's child Parikshit to identifying Parikshit and Madravati as Janamejaya's parents.
CURRENT identifies Satyavati as the parent of Dwaipayana Vyasa, offspring of Parasara; existing evidence identifies her son by Parasara as Dwaipayana.
Both identify Parasara through parentage of Dwaipayana Vyasa.

unresolved: pandu: CURRENT identifies only a Pandu whose children participated in the battle against Kuru's children. The existing excerpt identifies Pandu as a child of Dwaipayana; CURRENT does not corroborate that parentage or explicitly identify his children as the five Pandavas. The proposed identity remains uncertain.
unnamed_questioning_rishi: CURRENT never identifies the questioning Rishi as Saunaka. Attendance at Saunaka's sacrifice does not establish that identity.
